Pregnancy

PRP hair treatment during pregnancy: what is known?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Platelet-rich plasma treatment uses a preparation made from your own blood to treat selected areas of the scalp. It can sound reassuringly natural, but that does not answer the main pregnancy question: has the procedure been adequately studied for you and your developing baby? For elective hair restoration, the usual approach is to wait and first investigate the cause of the hair changes.

Start by finding out why the hair is changing

Hair shedding can affect confidence, especially when it arrives alongside the other changes of pregnancy. Before paying for a procedure, ask a clinician to examine the scalp and review the timing, pattern and severity of the loss. Gradual thinning at the part, sudden widespread shedding and a sharply defined bald patch can have different causes and need different care.

Pregnancy does not make every form of hair loss hormonal or harmless. A recent illness, nutritional deficiency, thyroid problem, scalp inflammation or medicine may be relevant. Tests are chosen from the history and examination rather than ordered automatically. Report a painful, inflamed or scarring scalp promptly, and mention eyebrow loss or other new symptoms.

Postpartum shedding is different from permanent thinning

Some people notice fuller hair during pregnancy, followed by increased shedding after delivery as hormone levels change. This temporary shedding often becomes most noticeable a few months after birth and may peak around four months. Most people regain their previous fullness by their baby’s first birthday, although individual recovery varies.

That pattern does not explain every case of hair loss during pregnancy or after birth. If loss is patchy, the scalp is abnormal, or fullness has not recovered after a year, seek an assessment. A treatment offered for inherited pattern hair loss should not automatically be sold as necessary for ordinary postpartum shedding.

What platelet-rich plasma actually contains

Platelet-rich plasma, usually called PRP, is prepared from a small sample of the person’s own blood. Platelets are cell fragments involved in clotting and wound repair. They contain signalling proteins, including growth factors, which are part of the reason clinicians have studied concentrated platelets in several treatment settings.

PRP has been used and investigated in areas such as wound care and some muscle, tendon, joint and ligament problems. Evidence from those uses does not establish that scalp injections work equally well, or that a cosmetic procedure is safe in pregnancy. The intended treatment, preparation method and patient group each need their own evidence.

How a scalp appointment is usually performed

A clinician draws blood and places it in a centrifuge, a machine that spins the sample to separate its components. Red blood cells and plasma fractions separate, allowing a platelet-enriched portion to be collected. Different systems produce different preparations; the name PRP does not describe one standard concentration or recipe.

The preparation is then injected into selected areas of the scalp, usually through several small needle punctures. Cleaning, preparation, blood collection and any numbing step add to the appointment time. Ask the clinic what its procedure includes rather than relying on a promise that every visit takes a particular number of minutes.

Some clinics combine PRP with microneedling, topical products or medicines. Those additions are separate exposures with separate questions about effectiveness and safety. Obtain the actual product names, including the numbing agent, rather than assuming the treatment consists only of your own blood.

Results take time and treatment usually needs repeating

PRP may help selected people with pattern hair loss, but regrowth is variable and it does not create an unlimited supply of new follicles. Studies and clinic protocols differ in preparation, injection technique, frequency and outcome measurements. A before-and-after photograph is not a guarantee of the result another person will achieve.

An initial series followed by maintenance visits is common. The American Academy of Dermatology describes one schedule of monthly treatment for three months, then appointments every three to six months. This is an example, not a universal prescription. Visible change can take several months, and some people do not obtain worthwhile improvement.

Discuss the total cost, how response will be measured and when treatment would be stopped if ineffective. Photographs taken with comparable lighting, parting and hair length are more useful than casual snapshots. Ask whether the expected benefit justifies repeated procedures alongside other appropriate options.

Why elective PRP is usually deferred during pregnancy

Using your own blood reduces some concerns associated with a foreign product, but it does not establish pregnancy safety. Direct evidence about elective cosmetic PRP in pregnant people is lacking. A recent dermatology review recommends deferring it during pregnancy unless there is a medical need requiring an individual assessment.

This recommendation reflects an evidence gap and the elective nature of hair restoration. It is not proof that PRP causes birth defects or pregnancy loss. Avoid both extremes: a clinic should not promise that it is completely safe because it is natural, and someone who has already had treatment should not be told that harm is inevitable.

Pregnancy is a reasonable time to clarify the diagnosis and use appropriate supportive hair care. If an underlying illness or deficiency is found, treating that condition may matter much more than a cosmetic procedure. Discuss when to reconsider PRP after birth, taking breastfeeding and any additional medicines into account.

Numbing medicines and accompanying treatments need their own review

Local anaesthetics are not all forbidden in pregnancy. For example, available human information on lidocaine has not identified an increased birth-defect risk, although not every pregnancy outcome or exposure pattern has been well studied. Suitability still depends on the product, dose, route, timing and reason for treatment.

That distinction matters: evidence about a numbing medicine does not make the whole elective PRP procedure proven safe. Likewise, advice about PRP does not replace advice about another hair treatment. Minoxidil and prescription anti-androgen treatments require specific pregnancy and breastfeeding discussion. Do not start them because they are bundled with a clinic package, or stop an essential medicine without speaking to its prescriber.

Know the possible procedural complications

Needle treatment can cause pain, tenderness, itching or burning, swelling, bruising, pinpoint bleeding or headache. These effects may settle, but their severity and duration vary. Infection, injury to a blood vessel or nerve, and a reaction to a numbing agent or another added product are additional concerns. Your own plasma does not remove risks related to injections, handling or equipment.

Tell the clinician about a bleeding disorder, low platelet count, scalp infection, allergies and every medicine or supplement you take, especially products that affect bleeding. Do not independently stop a prescribed blood thinner to make a cosmetic appointment possible. Ask who performs the procedure, how equipment and blood samples are handled, and what follow-up is available.

After any injection procedure, increasing redness, heat, swelling, discharge, fever or severe pain needs medical advice. Breathing difficulty, collapse or swelling of the mouth or throat is an emergency. A clinic’s description of treatment as minimally invasive should still include a clear complications plan.

Regulatory claims need careful wording

A blood-processing device can have regulatory clearance for a specified use without every advertised treatment made with that device being approved. Ask exactly which device or product a clinic is referring to and what indication its claim covers. PRP is a procedure involving a blood preparation, so a blanket statement about it being an approved hair-loss drug is misleading.

In the United States, the FDA states that it has not cleared microneedling devices for hair loss or reviewed their use in combination with another product, including PRP. Scalp injection and microneedling are also different procedures. Regulatory wording varies by country; a local registration number is not a substitute for evidence of benefit or pregnancy safety.

If you already had PRP while pregnant

Contact your maternity clinician with the treatment date, how far along the pregnancy was, the treated area, and the names of all injected, applied or prescribed products. Ask the clinic for the written record if you do not have these details. Include any reaction you experienced and any medicines used afterwards.

The team can assess the actual exposure and decide whether anything beyond usual care is needed. Do not assume that an elective treatment means the pregnancy has been harmed, and do not arrange repeated scans or blood tests on your own. For now, defer further cosmetic sessions until you have individual advice.

Make a practical plan for later

A dermatologist can help distinguish temporary shedding from a condition likely to persist and explain which options fit pregnancy, breastfeeding and future plans. Gentle handling, avoiding tight pulling styles, and limiting damaging heat or chemical treatments can reduce breakage, although they do not cure every cause of thinning.

At a later PRP consultation, ask what diagnosis is being treated, what benefit is realistic, which preparation will be used, whether other products are included, how many visits are expected and what happens if there is no response. Choose a decision based on the diagnosis and your priorities, rather than pressure to begin before the cause of the hair loss is clear.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Dermatology guidance describes PRP as a repeat treatment with variable benefit, not guaranteed permanent regrowth.

Pregnancy-specific cosmetic PRP outcome data are lacking; current expert guidance favours deferring elective treatment.

How BeMama can help

Keep the clinic’s product list and procedure record with your pregnancy notes, and discuss the cause of the hair change before booking treatment.

When to seek help

Seek care for a painful or inflamed scalp and report possible infection after injections. Breathing difficulty, collapse or mouth and throat swelling requires emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Your own blood does not make a procedure risk-free.
  • Pregnancy safety has not been established for elective cosmetic PRP.
  • Postpartum shedding often improves without hair-restoration treatment.
  • Numbing agents, minoxidil and other additions need separate assessment.
  • Check the diagnosis, realistic benefits, repeated costs and follow-up before deciding.

Frequently asked questions

Is PRP completely safe because it comes from my own blood?

No. Autologous blood reduces some concerns, but injections, sample handling and additional products still carry risks. Direct pregnancy safety evidence is also lacking.

Can I have scalp PRP during pregnancy?

Elective cosmetic PRP is generally deferred. Discuss the hair loss with your maternity clinician and a dermatologist so a treatable underlying cause is not missed.

Does this mean PRP is known to harm a developing baby?

No. Lack of adequate pregnancy data is different from proof of harm. The recommendation to wait reflects uncertainty and the elective purpose of treatment.

What happens during the appointment?

Blood is collected, spun to separate its components and used to prepare a platelet-rich portion for scalp injections. Numbing and additional products vary, so request the specific protocol.

Will three or four sessions definitely restore my hair?

No. Response and schedules vary. Some people benefit after several months; others do not. Maintenance treatment is often needed, and the underlying diagnosis matters.

Are all local anaesthetics unsafe in pregnancy?

No. Some, including lidocaine, have reassuring human pregnancy information for appropriate uses. That does not prove that an elective PRP package as a whole is safe or necessary.

Is PRP automatically suitable while breastfeeding?

No automatic rule applies. Expert guidance allows cautious individual consideration, but the diagnosis, numbing agent and any combined medicines still need review.

Does ordinary postpartum shedding need PRP?

Usually it improves as the hair cycle settles. Many people recover their usual fullness by the baby’s first birthday. Persistent, patchy or inflammatory loss deserves assessment.

What should I do if I already had a session before knowing I was pregnant?

Give your maternity clinician the date and full treatment record, including added products. They can assess the actual exposure without assuming that harm has occurred.

What should a clinic’s approval claim tell me?

It should identify the particular device or product, country and authorised indication. Device clearance does not establish pregnancy safety or guarantee that PRP works for hair loss.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
